extracted.intended_audience: Reporters, editors, photographers and all members of The New York Times news staff
extracted.subtask_description: Ethical and practical standards for producing journalism at The New York Times, covering accuracy, attribution, sourcing, corrections, use of anonymous sources, photography, and conflicts of interest. Intended to guide newsroom behavior and decision-making to preserve the paper's integrity and readers' trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protecting the newspaper's integrity and reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: "Our greatest strength is the authority and reputation of The Times. We must do nothing that would undermine or dilute it and everything possible to enhance it." Staff must maintain the highest possible standards to insure they do nothing that might erode readers’ faith and confidence in our news columns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be vigilant in avoiding any activity that might pose an actual or apparent conflict of interest; practice journalism beyond reproach. This is a general, overarching duty guiding all other specific rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding actual or apparent conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Staff members should be vigilant in avoiding any activity that might pose an actual or apparent conflict of interest and thus threaten the newspaper’s ethical standing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an activity could reasonably erode readers' trust or suggest partiality, it should be avoided or disclosed/managed in consultation with editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: No falsification
rubrics_metrics.description: Falsifying any part of a news report cannot be tolerated and will result automatically in disciplinary action up to and including termination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absolute prohibition on inventing facts, quotes, or details. Writers and editors must ensure factual authenticity at all stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotations accuracy and handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers should be able to assume that every word between quotation marks is what the speaker or writer said. The Times does not 'clean up' quotations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If grammar or taste is unsuitable, remove quotation marks and paraphrase. Omit extraneous syllables like 'um' and judiciously delete false starts; for further omissions close the quotation and begin another with new attribution. The Times adjusts spelling, punctuation, capitalization and abbreviations for consistent style. Writer and editor must both be satisfied that the intent of the subject has been preserved. Consult the stylebook entry 'quotations' for detailed guidance. Avoid 'approximate' quotations that could undermine trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution of other organizations' reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: When we use facts gathered by any other organization, we attribute them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This applies to newspapers, magazines, books, broadcasts and news agencies (e.g., 'the Senator told The Associated Press'). For pool reports, attribute to the pool reporter. In roundups, use phrases like 'reports from news agencies and New York Times bureaus.' Even AP reporting is not treated as our own. Preference is to verify and do our own reporting when time permits; if we verify independently we need not attribute the facts, but should credit exclusives to the organization that first broke the news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution does not excuse publishing rumors
rubrics_metrics.description: Attribution to another publication cannot serve as license to print rumors that would not meet The Times’s own reporting standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rumors must satisfy The Times’s standard of newsworthiness, taste and plausibility before publication, even when attributed. When in doubt about whether to publish attributed material, consult the department head.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing firsthand and indirect reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: In those cases when it makes a difference whether we directly witnessed a scene, we should distinguish in print between personal interviews and telephone or E-mail interviews, as well as written statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about the mode of information gathering when it materially affects the reader's understanding of the report's basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writers as principal fact-checkers
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers at The Times are their own principal fact checkers and often their only ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete facts (distances, addresses, phone numbers, people’s titles) must be verified by the writer with standard references (telephone books, directories, official web sites). More obscure checks may be referred to the research desk. If deadline pressure requires skipping a check, alert editors with a flag like 'desk, please verify' and ideally double back after filing. Always verify the spelling of names; misspellings damage trust and commonly generate corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrections policy
rubrics_metrics.description: The Times recognizes an ethical responsibility to correct all its factual errors, large and small.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any complaint should be relayed to a supervising editor and investigated quickly. If a correction is warranted, it should be published immediately. In case of reasonable doubt or disagreement, the paper can acknowledge that a statement was 'imprecise' or 'incomplete' even if not certain it was wrong. Writers who volunteer corrections are applauded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuttals and right of reply
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek and publish a response from anyone criticized in our pages, especially for serious criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When criticism is serious, describe the scope of the accusation and let the subject respond in detail. No subject should be taken by surprise or feel there was no chance to respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of anonymous sources and promises of anonymity
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of unidentified sources is reserved for situations in which the newspaper could not otherwise print information it considers newsworthy and reliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, reporter and editor should discuss any promise of anonymity before it is made. Some beats (criminal justice, national security) may have standing authorization. Tell readers as much as possible about the placement and known motivation of the source. Avoid automatic phrases like 'insisted on anonymity'—state tersely what understanding was reached. Be literally truthful and not coy: do not refer to a single person as 'sources' or say 'other officials' when someone has been cited by name. Use anonymity sparingly and transparently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fictionalization and concealment devices
rubrics_metrics.description: The Times refrains outright from assigning fictional names, ages, places or dates, and strictly limits the use of other concealment devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer to omit a name and explain the omission if identity must be shielded. For narratives requiring multiple shielded identities, use given names with last initials or given names alone; descriptions may serve instead. As a rare last resort, use single initials after consultation with senior editors. The article must gracefully indicate the device and the reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Masquerading and misrepresentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Times reporters do not actively misrepresent their identity to get a story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters may remain silent or allow assumptions (e.g., to observe behavior in public) but sustained, systematic deception—even passive deception like taking a job to observe—may be employed only after consultation with a department head and masthead editors. Specific exceptions exist (e.g., restaurant reviewing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity and manipulation of photography and images
rubrics_metrics.description: Images in our pages that purport to depict reality must be genuine in every way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No people or objects may be added, rearranged, reversed, distorted or removed from a scene (except cropping). Adjustments of color or gray scale should be limited to those minimally necessary for clear and accurate reproduction. Pictures of news situations must not be posed. For collages, montages, portraits, fashion or home design illustrations and contrived situations, intervention should be unmistakable and free of intent to deceive. Captions and credits should acknowledge intervention if doubt is possible. Consult the design director, a masthead editor or the news desk on doubtful cases or proposals for exceptions.
